edges.description: An external address used a remote desktop gateway to log in as jsmith on WKSTN-042, the first sign of unauthorized access.
Right after the suspicious login, a disguised PowerShell command was launched from Outlook on the same machine, typical of an attacker trying to run further tools quietly.
The workstation began sending small regular bursts of data back to the same outside address, consistent with the attacker keeping remote control of the machine.
Commands were run to see who the current user was and who belonged to the Domain Admins group, a step attackers take to plan further movement.
The memory of a core Windows security process was copied out, a common way to steal saved passwords and credentials from a machine.
Using a credential taken from the earlier password dump, the workstation requested a ticket for the administrator account from the domain controller without needing the real password.

edges.action: logged into file server as admin
edges.description: With the stolen administrator credential, the compromised workstation connected to the file server and opened a file-sharing session there.
A command window was started on the file server through a remote management technique, giving the attacker the ability to run further commands there.
Using the admin account, financial forecasts and a file of employee social security numbers were opened, showing the attacker was after valuable data.
The files gathered were compressed into a single archive in a temporary folder, preparing them to be moved out of the network.
A large encrypted transfer of about 480 megabytes went out from the file server to an outside address shortly after the archive was created, matching the size of stolen data leaving.
The file server sent a short message back to the same outside address used earlier, likely telling the attacker the data transfer had finished.
The Windows security log on the file server was cleared, removing much of the record of what had just happened.
The compressed file that had been prepared for transfer was deleted afterward, an attempt to remove evidence of the data collection.

summary: An external login to WKSTN-042 as jsmith led to credential theft and a pass-the-hash move to the domain controller as administrator, followed by data collection, exfiltration of roughly 480MB, and cleanup of logs and staged files on the file server.
